title: Santner Sets Out His Plan to Contain India's Power Hitters in T20 Series
excerpt: New Zealand's white-ball captain wants early Christchurch movement, wicket-taking intent on flat pitches, and treats two or three wickets for under 40 runs as a good spell against Abhishek, Ishan, Sanju and Sooryavanshi.
body:
• New Zealand white-ball captain Mitchell Santner says containing India's power hitters starts with early-season Christchurch movement if it is available, and with bigger boundaries and wicket-taking pressure if pitches are flat.
  • Santner named Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson and teenage IPL sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as the threats, saying India have power throughout the lineup.
  • His benchmark for a good spell against this lineup: two or three wickets for around 30 to under 40 runs, and keeping India near 200 would count as a good outcome in New Zealand.
  • The five-match T20I series is part of India's tour of New Zealand, which begins October 22 and also brings Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli for the ODIs.

New Zealand white-ball captain Mitchell Santner has laid out, in unusually specific terms, how his bowlers intend to approach India's top order in the five-match T20I series: use any early-season movement in Christchurch, accept that boundaries will come, and judge success by wickets and the balls in between rather than by dot-ball counts.

Santner, a left-arm spinner leading the Black Caps at home, named the problem plainly. Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan and Sanju Samson can dismantle an attack from the first over, and behind them stands Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the teenager whose IPL exploits Santner said he has watched closely. India, he said, have power throughout the lineup.

"If you can take two or three wickets for around 30 or even under 40 runs, you are probably doing a very good job."

— Mitchell Santner, New Zealand white-ball captain

Movement First, Boundaries Second

The first lever is conditions. Early-season pitches in Christchurch could offer movement, Santner said, and if the ball moves, New Zealand need to use that to counter India's explosive batting during the powerplay. The choice of weapon, he explained, has to be made ball by ball against hitters who come hard from the start: yorkers, arm balls, or taking the ball away from their hitting arc.

If the pitch is flat, the plan changes rather than disappears. New Zealand would then try to create pressure by using the bigger boundaries and finding different ways of taking wickets. Santner was blunt that boundaries are inevitable against this opposition; the contest, in his framing, is about what happens with the balls in between — whether they are wicket-taking deliveries or dots.

A Recalibrated Idea of a Good Spell

Santner's numbers underline how far T20 bowling economics have shifted. Conceding 30 to 40 runs in a four-over spell, he said, can now represent a good performance if it comes with two or three wickets. On totals, he set the home benchmark equally plainly: if New Zealand can restrict India to around 200 in New Zealand conditions, that could be a good score given the strength India possess.

Other coverage of Santner's remarks made the same broader point: bowlers are trying to catch up in a format that keeps tilting toward batters, and neutralising India's attack will require aggressive wicket-taking through the powerplay and middle overs rather than containment alone, Sports Wire Live reported on October 14.

History Between the Sides

Santner also acknowledged the recent history India carry into the tour. New Zealand's historic 3-0 Test series triumph on Indian soil and a 2-1 ODI series victory give India, in his words, a point to prove. His counter was that New Zealand's job is to play what is in front of them and beat a very good team at home, adding that the more his side plays in places like India, the better equipped it becomes to handle those conditions.

The tour is not only about the T20Is. Santner expects Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma to draw enormous attention in the ODI leg, remarking that the two senior batters may not be getting any younger but are still churning out the runs.

What to Watch

India's tour of New Zealand starts on October 22, 2026, with coverage on Sony Sports Network and Sony LIV, according to the Times of India report. The first tactical test of Santner's plan will be the Christchurch surface itself: if it offers the early movement he is counting on, New Zealand's new-ball bowlers get the contest he wants. If it is flat, the series becomes a test of his second plan — bigger boundaries, constant wicket-taking intent, and a bowling unit willing to treat 200 as a defendable line rather than a defeat.
